issues.legal_issue: Judicial review of a public corporation’s commercial selection decision between competing candidates requires caution and is justified only by substantial public interest or bad faith in the transaction.
material_facts: A public corporation selected a candidate ranked first for a retail outlet dealership, while a competing candidate ranked second challenged the selection through a writ petition.
The dispute was between rival candidates, and the Court found that the challenge was a deliberate attempt to deny the selected candidate the benefit of the selection.
The litigation delayed establishment of an outlet that could provide a service to the public, and no continuing lack of need for the outlet was shown.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should have exercised caution before intervening in the commercial selection dispute; intervention was not justified merely because a rival candidate raised a legal objection, absent substantial public interest or bad faith in the transaction.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226, a public authority’s commercial contract decision is reviewable for a decision-making process vitiated by mala fides, unreasonableness or arbitrariness, but judicial intervention in a dispute between rival tenderers or candidates requires substantial public interest or a transaction entered into mala fide. Courts should exercise their discretionary jurisdiction cautiously and in furtherance of public interest. The Court relied on Raunaq International Ltd. v. I.V.R. Construction Ltd. (1999) 1 SCC 492; Air India Ltd. v. Cochin International Airport Ltd. (2000) 2 SCC 617; and the related principles in Ramana Dayaram Shetty, Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union, CCE v. Dunlop India, Tata Cellular, Ramniklal N. Bhutta, Master Marine Services and Tejas Constructions.

rule.if: public_body_contract_selection_challenge and rival_candidates_dispute and substantial_public_interest_absent and transaction_bad_faith_absent

predicates.public_body_contract_selection_challenge: A party challenges through judicial review a public body’s decision selecting a contractor, dealer or other commercial awardee.
predicates.rival_candidates_dispute: The dispute is between competing candidates for the same commercial award.
predicates.substantial_public_interest_absent: The challenge does not establish a substantial public interest that warrants judicial intervention.
predicates.transaction_bad_faith_absent: The challenged commercial transaction was not shown to have been entered into in bad faith.

issues.definition: When a public-body selection challenge is only a dispute between rivals, and neither substantial public interest nor bad faith in the transaction is established, the rule yields that writ intervention is not warranted.

issues.legal_issue: Where material later evidence undermines the asserted obstacle to the highest-ranked candidate’s selection and the public service remains justified, the selection should not be displaced in favour of a lower-ranked rival.
material_facts: The appellant had ranked first in the selection, and the competing candidate had ranked second.

The selected site had initially been said to be involved in litigation, but the District Authority later sought further information, an official report recommended granting the required clearance, and the land was removed from the scope of the partition suit; the relevant suits were subsequently dismissed or withdrawn.
The High Court overlooked material documents concerning the clearance and the litigation over the site.
The Court found that the challenge was a deliberate attempt to deny the selected candidate the benefit of the selection and that the outlet’s public service remained needed.
issues.conclusion: The Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court’s orders, and directed the corporation to complete its prescribed formalities to award the dealership to the highest-ranked candidate if it considered operation of the outlet still justified.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the totality of the material evidence, including later developments concerning the proposed site and the land litigation, and applied the caution required in reviewing a public corporation’s commercial selection. It relied on Article 226 and the principles stated in Raunaq International Ltd. v. I.V.R. Construction Ltd. (1999) 1 SCC 492 and Air India Ltd. v. Cochin International Airport Ltd. (2000) 2 SCC 617. The direction remained subject to the corporation completing its own prescribed selection formalities and considering whether the outlet was still justified.

rule.if: appeal_from_review_of_public_selection and candidate_ranked_first and material_evidence_overlooked and site_obstacle_no_longer_supported and public_service_still_justified

predicates.appeal_from_review_of_public_selection: An appeal challenges a court’s review of a public body’s selection decision.
predicates.candidate_ranked_first: The candidate seeking the award was ranked first in the selection.
predicates.material_evidence_overlooked: The court below failed to consider material evidence relevant to the parties’ entitlement to the award.
predicates.site_obstacle_no_longer_supported: Later evidence showed that the asserted legal obstacle concerning the proposed site no longer prevented the site from being considered for the intended use.
predicates.public_service_still_justified: The public body considers that the proposed service remains justified by the public’s needs.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns review of a public selection, the candidate ranked first, overlooked evidence removes the supported basis for a site obstacle, and the service remains justified, the rule yields a direction to complete the award formalities for that candidate.
